scenes.narration: This chapter covers three services that solve genuinely different decoupling problems, not three names for the same thing. S Q S — Simple Queue Service — is a point-to-point buffer: one message, one consumer. S N S is publish-subscribe fan-out: one message, many independent subscribers. And EventBridge is a content-routed event bus for many producers and many consumers, third-party software-as-a-service partners included. This maps to Design Resilient Architectures on the associate exam, twenty six percent of that exam, and Design for New Solutions on the professional exam, twenty nine percent — decoupling is one of the most consistently tested resilience techniques on both.

facts.value: Standard for throughput · FIFO for strict order + exactly-once, within a message group

facts.label: Amazon SNS → fan out to SQS
facts.value: One publish, one independent copy per subscribed queue

scenes.narration: Here's the trap. A scenario needs one order-placed event to reach fulfillment, analytics, and notifications, so the tempting design drops a single S Q S queue in the middle and assumes each of the three systems will just read the messages it cares about. A second, quieter trap: treating S N S as the universal decoupling hammer, reaching for it even in scenarios that are really just one producer feeding one consumer that needs buffering — a plain S Q S problem. Both instincts feel like decoupling. Only one of them actually solves the stated problem.

props.heading: "One queue can broadcast to everyone"
bullets: Put a single SQS queue between one producer and three consumer systems, assuming each just reads what it cares about.
Reach for SNS by reflex whenever a scenario says "decouple," even for one producer feeding one consumer that just needs buffering.
Assume any queue scales by simply adding more independent listeners of different kinds.

scenes.narration: Walk through why the first instinct fails. An S Q S queue implements competing consumers: each message goes to exactly one consumer, then gets deleted. Put three independent systems on the same queue, and each message is claimed by whichever one gets there first — the other two simply never see it. The real fix is an S N S topic publishing once, fanning out to three separate S Q S queues, one per consumer system, each buffered and consumed at its own pace. And the second trap runs the other way: S N S has no buffering of its own beyond a limited retry policy, so a single producer feeding a single logical consumer is still squarely an S Q S problem. EventBridge only enters once you've got many event types and many producers — including outside software-as-a-service partners — that need routing by the event's own content.

props.kicker: WHY IT'S WRONG, AND THE FIX
props.heading: Point-to-point vs fan-out vs content-routed
steps: SQS is competing consumers — each message delivered to and deleted by exactly one consumer, never all of them
Three pollers on one queue split the traffic three ways; two of them never see most messages
The fix: an SNS topic publishing once, fanning out to three separate SQS queues — one full copy each
SNS has no polling model and only a limited retry policy — a single producer/consumer needing buffering is still an SQS job
EventBridge takes over once producers and event types multiply, including third-party SaaS partners routed by content

scenes.narration: This table resolves most of the chapter's scenario questions. One producer, one logical consumer needing buffering: S Q S Standard. Same shape, but the requirement says strict order or exactly-once: S Q S FIFO. One event that several independent consumer systems each need their own copy of: S N S fanning out to multiple S Q S queues. Many event types from many producers — your own services plus third-party software-as-a-service partners — routed by the event's own content: EventBridge. And whenever a message keeps failing and must never silently block the rest of the queue or simply vanish: a dead-letter queue behind a redrive policy. Real questions rarely name the service outright — they describe the requirement, and expect you to map it to this row.

props.heading: The single most exam-relevant table in this chapter

scenes.narration: Standard and FIFO get confused on purpose, so isolate exactly what differs. Standard delivers at-least-once with best-effort order — duplicates are rare but possible, and that's fine when correctness doesn't depend on exact ordering. FIFO guarantees strict order and exactly-once processing, but only within a single message group — different groups, say different customer accounts, still process in parallel — and that guarantee costs some throughput ceiling versus Standard, though batching narrows the gap considerably. The exam's signal is never a specific number; it's the words "strict order," "exactly once," or "no duplicates" sitting inside the requirement.

props.kicker: THE PAIR THE EXAM CONFUSES ON PURPOSE

cells: Order or exactly-once is a correctness requirement

scenes.narration: A handful of facts decide most of the remaining trap questions. All three services cap a standard message around two hundred fifty six kilobytes — for S Q S, the Extended Client Library is the standard answer for a larger payload, storing the body in S3 and passing a reference through the queue. Delivery is at-least-once, so your consumer needs to be safe running twice on the same message. If real processing time runs longer than the visibility timeout, the message becomes visible again and a second consumer can pick it up — raise the timeout, or extend it dynamically. And the standard answer for a message that keeps failing is a redrive policy: its max-receive-count setting decides how many attempts happen before the message moves to a dead-letter queue — a D L Q — so nothing blocks the rest of the traffic and nothing is silently lost.

props.kicker: LIMITS, EDGE CASES & THE STANDARD FAILURE ANSWER
props.heading: What the correct answer still has to respect
bullets: All three cap a standard message/event around 256 KB — the SQS Extended Client Library offloads larger payloads to S3.
At-least-once delivery means your consumer has to be idempotent — safe to run twice on the same message.
If real processing time exceeds the visibility timeout, a second consumer can pick up and reprocess the same message.
A redrive policy's maxReceiveCount decides how many attempts happen before a message moves to its dead-letter queue.
An SNS subscription filter policy lets one subscriber ask for only the messages it needs, without splitting into more topics.

scenes.narration: Here's how the fan-out pipeline is actually organized, one file per intent. A single topic config for the order-placed event. Three separate queue definitions — fulfillment, analytics, notifications — each its own resource, not a shared one. One redrive-policy file, because the max-receive-count-plus-dead-letter-queue shape is identical across all three queues. And a separate EventBridge folder entirely, holding the partner bus that ingests third-party shipping events and the content-based rule that routes them — a genuinely different mechanism sitting right alongside the SNS fan-out, not a replacement for it.

props.heading: fanout-pipeline/
lines: ├── redrive-policy.json          # maxReceiveCount + DLQ ARN, shared shape

scenes.narration: None of these exact flags matter for the exam — what matters is which decision each command expresses. Creating the topic, then subscribing a queue: that subscribe call is the moment one producer becomes three independent copies, and you repeat it once per consumer system, with zero changes to the topic or the producer. Creating a queue with FifoQueue true turns on strict ordering; sending a message with a message-group-id of the account number is what keeps that one account's transactions strictly ordered, while other accounts' groups still process in parallel. And events put-rule is EventBridge's content-based routing in action — matching only on a partner's shipment-status field, something neither S Q S nor a plain S N S filter policy is built to do across a growing set of outside producers.

props.heading: Standing up the fan-out, and the FIFO ordering key

steps.cmd: aws sns subscribe --topic-arn arn:...:order-placed --protocol sqs --notification-endpoint arn:...:fulfillment-queue
output: Subscription created — repeat once per queue
Each subscriber gets its own full, independent copy
FIFO queue created — ordering + exactly-once apply per message group
MessageId returned — this account's transactions now process strictly in order
Rule created — matches only delayed-shipment events from the partner bus

scenes.narration: Take a concrete case. Northgate's order service needs the same order-placed event to independently trigger fulfillment, analytics, and customer notifications, with a hard requirement that any one of those three being slow or briefly offline can never affect the other two. Run it through the framework: one event, three independent consumer systems, each needing its own durable copy — that's not a bigger queue, it's an S N S topic fanning out to three separate S Q S queues, one per system, each with its own dead-letter queue. It's the single most heavily tested architecture across both exams, and it's exactly this shape.

Second, sharper one: a company is routing events from its own services and a third-party shipping partner, targeting different systems by the event's own content, with both sides of that expected to keep growing — why does EventBridge beat S N S here specifically?

questions.prompt: A single SQS queue sits between an order service and three downstream systems — fulfillment, analytics, and notifications — each expecting every order event. In testing, each system only receives about a third of the events. Why?
options: SQS silently drops two-thirds of messages under load
Each message is delivered to exactly one consumer — competing consumers — so with three pollers, each message goes to whichever gets there first
The queue needs FIFO mode enabled to deliver to multiple consumers
Each consumer needs its own AWS account to receive a full copy

questions.prompt: A company routes events from its own microservices and a third-party shipping SaaS partner, targeting different internal systems based on fields inside each event, with producers and consumers both expected to keep growing. Why is EventBridge the better fit than SNS here?
options: SNS cannot accept subscriptions from more than a handful of consumers
EventBridge matches rules on the event's own content across a heterogeneous, growing set of producers and consumers, including a partner bus for third-party SaaS events
SNS messages cannot be consumed by AWS Lambda, only EventBridge's can
EventBridge guarantees exactly-once delivery while SNS never does

scenes.narration: Here's why. The single-queue design isn't a misconfiguration to fix — it's the fundamental contract S Q S makes: one message, one consumer, then deleted. A single queue can scale identical workers doing the same job faster, but it cannot deliver one message to three different, independent consumer systems; the fix is an S N S topic fanning out to three separate S Q S queues. And the shipping-partner scenario turns on scale and heterogeneity: S N S's model is a fixed topic with subscribers that get everything, narrowed only by a coarse filter policy, while EventBridge's rules engine is built specifically for many event types and many producers — your own services plus outside software-as-a-service partners — routed to many targets by content, which is exactly the shape that keeps growing here.

answers.prompt: Why did each of the three consumers only see about a third of the order events?
answers.correct: SQS is competing consumers — each message goes to exactly one poller, never all three.
answers.rationale: This isn't a misconfiguration to fix, it's the fundamental contract SQS makes: one message, one consumer, then deleted. A single queue can scale identical workers doing the same job faster, but it cannot deliver one message to three different, independent consumer systems. The fix is an SNS topic fanning out to three separate SQS queues, one per system.

answers.prompt: Why is EventBridge the better fit than SNS for the shipping-partner scenario?
answers.correct: EventBridge routes by the event's own content across a large, heterogeneous, growing set of producers and consumers — including a partner bus for third-party SaaS events.
answers.rationale: SNS's model is a fixed topic with subscribers that get everything, narrowed only by a coarse filter policy. EventBridge's rules engine is built specifically for many event types and many producers — your own services plus outside SaaS partners — routed to many different targets by content, which is exactly the shape that keeps growing here.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. S Q S is point-to-point, competing consumers — one message, one consumer — and that's exactly why it can't broadcast to independent systems by itself. S N S fanning out to multiple S Q S queues is the standard, heavily tested fix whenever several independent systems each need their own copy of the same event. EventBridge takes over once you're routing many event types from many producers — your own plus third-party software-as-a-service partners — by the event's own content. FIFO trades some throughput for strict order and exactly-once processing, but that guarantee only holds within a single message group. And a dead-letter queue behind a redrive policy is the standard, explicit answer whenever a message must never silently vanish or block everything behind it. Next up: chapter twelve, where this same decoupling idea reappears as CloudFront's origin flexibility and Route 53's routing policies — letting the backend change without ever changing the client-facing contract.

props.heading: What to remember from this chapter
takeaways: SQS is point-to-point, competing consumers — one message, one consumer — which is exactly why it can't broadcast to independent systems on its own.
SNS fanning out to multiple SQS queues is the standard, heavily tested pattern for one event reaching several independent consumer systems.
EventBridge takes over once you're routing many event types from many producers, including third-party SaaS partners, by the event's own content.
SQS FIFO trades some throughput for strict order and exactly-once processing, but only within a single message group.
A dead-letter queue with a redrive policy is the standard, explicit answer whenever a message must never be silently lost or allowed to block everything behind it.
